ch21.title: The End of Judas
ch21.b001: Outside the Chamber of Hewn Stone
ch21.b002: At half past eight on Friday morning the outer courts of the temple were full of the din of the preparation day: men shouting as they dragged their lambs along, hooves clattering on the paving stones, smoke drifting up from the direction of the altar. Judas Iscariot passed through the noise and went farther in. On the way he straightened his garments once. It was an old habit; he had always done it before entering a room where something important would happen. The councilors had gathered in their usual meeting place, the hall of hewn stone, and Caiaphas was reporting to them on the trial of the night. Judas stopped outside the chamber and waited for his name to be called.
ch21.b003: He had not slept at all. Each time he shut his eyes he saw the torches swaying among the olive trees of Gethsemane. He tried to cover that picture with another. He saw the councilors calling him into the middle of the hall; he saw them rising one after another to praise the man who had delivered up the Galilean who was endangering the nation. He wanted to believe he had done his people a great service. But through the night that belief had cracked again and again. Every time he thought of the Master standing bound before Caiaphas, and then before Pilate, something in his chest stung as if a needle had gone into it. He called the pain weariness.
ch21.b004: A hand tapped him lightly on the shoulder. It was a servant of the high priest. The man drew him just outside the hall and held out a small bag. He had been appointed to pay Judas for the betrayal of Jesus, he said, as though it were the most ordinary errand in the world, and here was his reward. The bag was heavy. Thirty pieces of silver. It was what a man would pay for a good, healthy slave.
ch21.b005: Judas knew that price. He was a man who reckoned. From the years when he had helped in his father’s business in Jericho, through more than three years of carrying the purse for the apostles, he had lived with the price of everything written in his head: a measure of barley, a basket of dried fish, a donkey, a slave. Now that figure lay in the palm of his hand. For a while he could not speak. Then he rushed back toward the door of the hall. The doorkeeper barred his way. He said he had something to say to the councilors, but the door did not open.
ch21.b006: They were not going to praise him. They were not even going to call him in. He stood outside the door with the price of a slave in his hand. Judas could not believe it: that they had let him betray his friends and his Master and then held out this as his wage. He walked out of the temple, or rather was carried out of it, like a man in a trance. Hardly aware of what he was doing, he let the bag fall into the deep pocket inside his cloak, the very place where for three years he had carried the purse that fed thirteen men.
ch21.b008: The streets were crowded, and Judas drifted along with the people. He did not need to ask where they were going. They were going to watch the crucifixions. He let himself be pushed along with them, north, toward the Damascus gate. Someone jostled his shoulder; someone laughed. He heard none of it. With every step the silver in his deep pocket knocked against his thigh. Once for each step, as if it were counting something.
ch21.b009: He tried not to think. The thoughts came anyway. The winter grass on the highlands north of Capernaum. The twelve of them kneeling in a circle, and the hands that came to rest on his head first of all. Those hands had not been heavy. They had felt like hands lifting something up. At the time he had tried to reckon why he was the first: an honor, or a worry? He had never settled the question. Now the answer came to him. It came much too late.
ch21.b010: And then last night. The Master had gone around the table washing the feet of the twelve, and he had washed Judas’s feet too, without the least haste, exactly as he washed the others’. He remembered also the hand that held out a morsel of bread dipped in the dish. To the very end those hands had treated him the same as everyone else. That was the hardest thing of all for Judas to bear. If the Master had once rebuked him, had once named him in front of the others and cast him out, he could have leaned on that anger and stayed standing. But all he had been given, right to the end, was the same steady treatment as any of them.
ch21.b011: Then something earlier. The feast at Bethany, the day a woman broke an expensive box of ointment over the Master. Judas had called it waste: money that could have gone to the poor. As a man who kept accounts, he had believed it an honest remark. When the Master set it aside in front of everyone, his face had burned. That day everything that had piled up in him for so long rose up at once: the feeling of being slighted, the sense of always standing a little outside among these Galileans, the suspicion that this man was afraid to assert his own power. He had resolved to get even, though with whom he did not know. And he had poured it all out on the one man who had done him no wrong. Now he saw it. What he had been reckoning that day was not the price of the ointment. It was the price of his own wounds.
ch21.b012: He clung to one more thought. Perhaps at the last moment the Master would show his power. Perhaps he would come down from the cross of his own accord. Even while he was laying his plans, Judas had sometimes held that idea in front of him like a shield. Then he would not be a traitor at all; he would be the man who had forced the hidden power into the open. It was a cowardly hope, and Judas knew it. But he could not let go of it, and he kept walking toward Golgotha.
ch21.b013: In the distance he could see the low hill of Golgotha. Judas looked at it over the shoulders of the crowd. Soldiers were hauling on ropes, and a crossbeam was rising slowly up the post. He knew who hung from it. In that moment something inside him gave way. He turned and ran: shoving through the people, back against the stream at the gate, retracing the whole way to the temple.
ch21.b014: This time he pushed straight past the doorkeeper. The councilors were still sitting. Judas stood before them. He was so out of breath that the words would hardly come. He stammered that he had sinned by betraying innocent blood. They had insulted him, he said; they had offered him the price of a slave as payment for his service. He repented of what he had done. Here was their money. He wanted to be free of the guilt of this thing.
ch21.b015: The councilors laughed at him. One who sat near where he stood waved him toward the door and told him that his Master had already been put to death by the Romans, and as for his guilt, what was that to them? That was his affair. Let him be gone. Judas heard it. He knew then that the reckoning was closed. No one would take this debt off his hands. As he left the chamber he pulled the silver out of the bag and flung it across the temple floor. The coins rolled and scattered in every direction, and for a while the sound of them echoed off the stone before it stopped.
ch21.b017: He walked out of the temple. Nothing held him now: not hope, not anger, not reckoning. All that was left was himself. What he had done had seemed so reasonable while he was doing it. There had been heat in the idea of revenge, and a thrill in plotting something dangerous. Now that heat had gone cold. Only the bare facts lay in front of him. He had sold the man who loved him. And he had gained nothing by it.
ch21.b018: The man who had once been an ambassador of the kingdom of heaven walked the streets of Jerusalem alone. No one recognized him. The apostles were in hiding. And even had they not been, there was not one face among them he could have gone to. For more than three years he had eaten and slept under the same roof as the eleven, and he had never once opened his heart to any of them. Not even to the Master had he ever gone with a trouble of his own. When he was in distress he had always looked for comfort elsewhere, among relatives who knew nothing of the kingdom, among chance acquaintances. Now he could not even call their faces to mind.
ch21.b019: Andrew’s face crossed his mind for a moment. Andrew by the fire in the garden, watching him for a long time as he sat alone under the fig tree. Andrew had not come over that night. If he had, what would he have said? And what would Judas have answered? He could not follow the question to its end.
ch21.b020: Nathaniel’s face came to him too. Nathaniel had been the first to speak to him, at Tarichea, when he was looking for work near the fish-drying sheds at the lower end of the lake. It was Nathaniel who had brought him into the twelve. That day the Master had looked at him and said that they were all of one flesh, and that he prayed Judas would always be loyal to his Galilean brethren. Judas had thought at the time that it sounded like a welcome and a warning at once. Now he knew it had not been a warning. It had been a prayer. From beginning to end, a prayer for him. And he had never once taken it as his own.
ch21.b021: He went out through the walls and down to the south, into the valley of Hinnom. Smoke from the burning refuse lay low along the valley floor. It was a place where no one came.
ch21.b022: He climbed the steep rocks. He loosened the girdle of his cloak. One end he tied to a small tree rooted in a crack in the rock; the other he tied around his neck. His hands were trembling. They were the hands that had kept the accounts so neatly all his life, the hands that had never once tied the purse strings carelessly. He threw himself over the edge. But the knot his shaking hands had tied did not hold. Before he was dead it slipped, and his body fell onto the jagged rocks below.
ch21.b023: That was the end of Judas of Kerioth. The only Judean among the twelve, probably the best educated of them, a treasurer no one had ever faulted. There was no one in the valley where he fell. No one in Jerusalem wept for him that day. And Judas never knew that there had been one who did not abandon him to the last; that the man hanging at that hour on the hill north of the walls did not condemn him, but only pitied him.
ch21.b025: John Zebedee was not in the city that morning. As the Master was being taken off to Herod, he had turned to John and told him there was nothing more John could do for him now; he should go to his mother and bring her, so that she could see him before he died. John hated to leave him alone among his enemies. But he asked no questions and turned away. He had been the one apostle who stayed near the Master all night. And now he was the one apostle who had been told to leave him.
ch21.b026: He ran to Bethany. As he crossed the shoulder of the Mount of Olives, the sun climbed high. When he reached the home of Martha and Mary, the family of Jesus had arrived there only a few minutes earlier. Without stopping to catch his breath, John told them everything that had happened since the arrest at midnight: the arrest, Annas, Caiaphas, Pilate. The whole time he spoke, Mary the mother of Jesus never once interrupted him. When he had finished, she rose at once. Ruth, the Master’s sister, would not hear of staying behind, and so her brother Jude went along to look after her. The rest of the family stayed in Bethany, as James, the eldest brother, directed.
ch21.b027: By the time the four of them reached the city, the procession had already arrived at Golgotha. John helped Mary up the hill. The cross had only just been raised. The Roman captain was nailing a small white board above the Master’s head: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews, written in three languages. The sound of the hammer carried across the hill. John never forgot that sound.
ch21.b028: The cross was not high. The Master’s feet were only about three feet from the ground. So John could see his face clearly, and could see what he was looking at. At the foot of the cross four soldiers were dividing his clothes among them, as the custom was. One took the sandals, one the turban, one the girdle, one the cloak. That left the tunic, the seamless garment that reached nearly to the knees. The soldiers were about to cut it into four, but when they saw how unusual a garment it was they decided to cast lots for it instead. John knew that tunic. He had seen it for years along the roads of Galilee. The Master looked down while they divided his clothes, and the crowd around him jeered. John clenched his fists and let them go again. There was nothing at all he could do.
ch21.b029: The Master looked down at them: his mother, his brother, his sister, and John. He smiled, and said nothing. John received that smile. He could make no answer to it. But he knew what he had to do. Leaving Ruth and Jude at Mary’s side, he ran back down into the city. His own mother, Salome, and her companions were somewhere inside the walls waiting for news. They should be here too.
ch21.b030: While he was gone, something happened on the hill that John did not see. One of the thieves crucified beside the Master asked to be remembered, and the Master promised him that he would one day be with him in Paradise. John heard the story only later. He envied that thief, and he was not ashamed of envying him. John had been the youngest, the one who for so long had quietly prided himself on his place at the Master’s side. That day he learned that the place was open to anyone, even to a robber who turned to him at the very end.
ch21.b031: It was just after that promise that John came back, bringing nearly a dozen women believers with him. He took his place beside Mary and held her up. Her son Jude stood on her other side. It was noon. The Master looked down on them. He told his mother that John was now her son, and told John that she was now his mother. Then he asked them both to leave the place.
ch21.b032: John took the words into his hands. They were an entrusting. He had been given the Master’s mother to care for. Of the eleven, he was the only one given that charge. When its weight settled on his shoulders, he understood at last why he was on this hill. With Jude, he led Mary down from Golgotha. He brought her to the place where he was staying in Jerusalem, and then he ran back up the hill.
ch21.b034: A little after noon the sky turned a dirty yellow. It was early in the season for it, but a hot wind was blowing in from the Arabian desert, full of sand. Before one o’clock the sun was hidden. The onlookers hurried back into the city. On the hill there remained only thirteen Roman soldiers and about fifteen believers. Nearly all the believers were women. Only two were men: Jude, the Master’s brother, and John, who had come back just before the end.
ch21.b035: The sand stung their faces. The soldiers crouched together near the cross, huddled against the wind. Salome and the other women watched from a little way off, sheltered by an overhanging rock. John stood at the foot of the cross. With him were Jude, the Master’s brother, Ruth, his sister, Mary Magdalene, and Rebecca, onetime of Sepphoris. Now and then the Master’s lips moved. They were the Psalms. Most of the words were too faint to become sound; only a few pierced the wind and reached John’s ears.
ch21.b036: At about half past one the Master said, a second time, that he was thirsty. The captain of the guard soaked the sponge in the sour wine, fixed it on the point of a javelin, and moistened his lips. John watched the Roman’s hand. Perhaps it was the same hand that had nailed up the board that morning; now it moved carefully. John could not hate the man. He had no strength left for hatred. No, it was more than that: something in him would no longer take hatred in.
ch21.b037: It was just before three. The Master cried out in a loud voice that it was finished, and that he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands. Then he bowed his head. Only the sound of the wind was left. The centurion, who had watched how he died, struck his breast and said that this was indeed a righteous man; truly he must have been a Son of God. John heard him. It was a confession from the mouth of the Roman who had nailed the Master to the cross.
ch21.b038: John did not weep. He could not. He only stood there. He was twenty-eight. Four years before, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, he had laid down his nets beside his father Zebedee and stood up to follow. Back then he had been secretly proud to be one of the three closest to the Master, and that pride had followed him a long way. Now it was nowhere. There was nothing at all to be proud of in being the one who had stayed to the end. He was only grateful: grateful that he had been able to stand here, in the place of the other ten as well as his own.
ch21.b040: After the Master died, John asked Jude to take the women to the home of Elijah Mark. He himself stayed. By now the centurion knew him, and so he was allowed to remain. Before long three soldiers sent by Pilate arrived and broke the legs of the two thieves. They came to the Master and were surprised to find him already dead. To make sure, one of them drove his spear into his left side. John did not look away.
ch21.b041: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus came up the hill with an order from Pilate. The men sent by the Sanhedrin set up a clamor; they wanted the body dragged off to the pits where criminals were thrown. The centurion called four of his soldiers, and they stood with drawn swords over the Master’s body where it lay on the ground. When order returned, the centurion read out Pilate’s permit and told Joseph that the body was his. John looked at the Roman again. In one day he had seen more kindness from enemies than he could account for.
ch21.b042: At half past four, four men lifted the body wrapped in a linen sheet: Joseph and Nicodemus, the centurion, and John. John took the weight on his shoulder. It was lighter than he had expected. No, heavier. He could not tell which. Joseph’s new tomb, cut from the rock across the road, was only a short way off. John counted the steps one by one. If he did not count something he thought he would sink down where he stood. The women from Galilee followed at a distance, keeping out of sight.
ch21.b043: Bandages soaked in myrrh and aloes were wound about the body. A napkin was tied about the face. They laid the body on a shelf in the tomb. The soldiers rolled the great doorstone across the entrance; it rumbled low in its groove as it went. The Sabbath was coming on fast. The men hurried back into the city. Before he turned away, John looked once more at the tomb. He did not remember that the Master had spoken of the third day. That day he remembered nothing. He knew only that walking away from that stone was the hardest step of his life.
ch21.b044: The women stayed. Since women were not permitted to mingle with the men at such a time, they had hidden themselves close by and watched it all. Mary Magdalene; Mary the wife of Clopas; Martha, another sister of the Master’s mother; Rebecca of Sepphoris. They did not leave the tomb until it was quite dark. To their eyes the body had not been properly prepared. They agreed among themselves to make ready spices and ointments after the Sabbath and come back. John knew nothing of that agreement. None of the men going back into the city that night knew that at dawn on the third day Mary Magdalene and the other women would walk this road again.
ch21.b046: Simon Zelotes spent that day in a hiding place in the city. Thomas, Andrew, and James Zebedee were each hidden somewhere within the walls as well. Nathaniel, Matthew, Philip, and the twins were scattered at Bethpage and Bethany. Peter had been sent at dawn to join his brother Andrew at the home of Nicodemus. David Zebedee, who had moved a few tents up the ravine above the Gethsemane camp, sent messengers with the news about every half hour. The scattered men counted out the day by the footsteps of those messengers.
ch21.b047: Every time a messenger came, Simon leaped to his feet. And every time he heard the news, he sank down again. Pilate had handed him over. They had taken him to Golgotha. At half past nine he had been put on the cross. Simon sat with his back against the wall and buried his head between his knees. He thought of himself the night before, standing on the stone wall of the olive press. He had called out to his fellows to go after the mob and rescue the Master. When they left the camp that afternoon, only Peter and he had been girded with swords. He had been ready to use his.
ch21.b048: Nathaniel had stood up to stop him. He reminded them of the nonresistance the Master had taught them over and over, and of how that very night the Master had told them to preserve their lives for the day they would go out into the world with the gospel. James Zebedee backed him: when Peter drew his sword, the Master had made him put it away. Last of all Thomas spoke. The Master would not let his friends defend him, he said, and he would not use his divine power either; they could not save him. Let them scatter. Simon climbed down from the wall. He could not answer any of it. That made it worse.
ch21.b049: After noon a messenger came again. The sky had gone dark with the sandstorm. The messenger said it briefly: just before three, the Master had died. Simon made no sound. For a long time he could not understand the words. He had given up a high place among the Zealots and followed this man while his old comrades called him a traitor. Wait, he had told them; this man is different. What would he tell them now? No: he had nothing left to say to anyone.
ch21.b050: What had drawn him to this man was his calm. The composure nothing could shake, the poise that could not be explained. Simon had believed it was the ease of a man holding great power in reserve, power that would show itself when the hour came. But the calm stayed calm to the end. Without lifting a sword, without calling up a single army, he had died. For the first time Simon doubted what that composure had been. And the doubt frightened him, because now he no longer knew what it was he had loved.
ch21.b051: He remembered the day on the highland when he had embraced the Master. He had hugged him roughly, the way a fighter hugs a comrade, and the Master had simply let himself be held. When the hands had rested on his head that day, Simon had clenched his teeth, as if bracing against something. But those hands had not put a sword into his. Something in him had loosened a little then, and it had frightened him. Now he thought he understood that fear. Those hands had never meant to give him a sword. He had known it and pretended not to. For four years he had bent the Master’s words to fit his own dream. Not by force of arms became not yet; turn the other cheek became wait for the right time. Now there were no words left to bend.
ch21.b052: The next day was the Sabbath. Simon looked out through the small window of his hiding place at the street. For the Passover week nearly a million and a half Jews had come into Jerusalem from every corner of the empire and from Mesopotamia. The voices of pilgrims passing below drifted up to the window. They were talking about the Galilean who had died on Golgotha the day before. One clicked his tongue; one laughed; another cursed Pilate for hanging up a board calling the man the king of the Jews. Simon listened, gripping the hilt of his sword. There was nothing left to use it for. He laid it down. He did not pick it up again that day.
ch21.b053: At the home of Nicodemus, Peter lay facing the wall. Andrew sat beside him. Peter had hardly spoken since dawn. Andrew did not ask what had happened; his brother’s face had already told him everything. He thought of laying a hand on Peter’s shoulder, and then thought better of it. Just now even that hand might be too heavy. Instead he sat there. Each time a messenger came in, it was Andrew who rose to take the news and then came back to sit down again beside his brother. That was all Andrew could give him that day.
ch21.b055: They spent the Sabbath in hiding while the whole city buzzed with talk of the Galilean who had died on the cross. Late on Saturday night John Mark sent quietly for the eleven apostles to come to his father’s house. Just before midnight they were all gathered in the upper room, the same room where two nights earlier they had eaten the last supper with the Master. The low U-shaped table and the couches they had reclined on were still in their places.
ch21.b056: They looked at one another. No one spoke first. The room was full of fear and grief and shame. They had all run away. Only John had stayed to the end. John sat in a corner. He did not tell them what he had seen, and no one asked. To ask would have meant telling where they themselves had been. Thomas came in, looked them over for a little while, and then without a word turned and went out again. No one tried to stop him.
ch21.b057: And the news of Judas was in that room. None of them could remember exactly when it had come or by whose mouth. They simply knew: he had died in the valley of Hinnom. The eleven sat stunned. They had been ready to hate him. Since they had seen that kiss in Gethsemane their hearts had been full of anger. And now he was dead. With the man gone, the hatred had nowhere to go. Something else came in to take its place, and they did not know what to call it.
ch21.b058: Peter shuddered. In the end of Judas he saw himself. He too had abandoned the Master, three times over, by the charcoal fire in the courtyard of Annas. How great was the distance between Judas and himself? He could not measure it. Matthew bowed his head. For three years the two of them had sat at the same table counting money. One had guarded the apostles’ funds; the other had raised them. Matthew knew that Judas had never once made a mistake in his figures. What he had been reckoning at the last, when it broke him, Matthew could not tell.
ch21.b059: The twins, James and Judas, sat side by side. They did not understand all that had happened. But they understood that a man had died, a man they had eaten with and walked the roads with. Judas Alpheus said the name quietly. Judas. It was his own name too. James took his hand. Philip looked as though he wanted to ask something, but in the end he did not; he could not even tell what the question would be. James Zebedee sat with his mouth set hard and looked across at his brother John. Nathaniel, who at a moment like this would usually have found something to say, found nothing that night.
ch21.b060: Andrew looked at the empty place at the table, the seat of honor at the Master’s left, the place Judas had stepped forward to claim two nights before. Andrew remembered, long ago on the highland, a hand idly plucking at blades of grass. He remembered a face lit on only one side by the fire in the garden. He remembered a dawn when Judas had sat alone under the fig tree, looking at the eastern sky. He had not gone over to him then, because he had not known what to say. Of all the twelve, Andrew had been the first to see that trouble was brewing in Judas. And he had told no one. Not to speak of what he was not sure of was his way. Whether that way had been right, he would now never know.
ch21.b061: Simon Zelotes lay down on one of the couches at the side of the room and turned his face to the wall. No one disturbed him. The lamp burned low and wavered. It was nearly midnight. The Sabbath had ended at sundown. Before the tomb lay two stones now, sealed with the seal of Pilate, and twenty men stood guard there. The ten in the upper room knew nothing of that. All they knew was that the Master was dead, and that the twelve were no longer even eleven.
ch21.b062: That night John lay awake a long time. He thought of the hill of Golgotha, of the sandstorm, of the stone that closed the tomb. And he thought of one thing more. The day on the grassy highland when the twelve had embraced the Master one by one. When the Master held Judas, his arms had held him no shorter and no longer than any of the others. John had not noticed it at the time. Now he saw it. To the very end, the Master had treated Judas the same. In the dark, for the first time, John wept for Judas. Not for the traitor, but for a man who had never been able to let himself be held.
ch21.b064: The course of events follows Papers 186–188. Judas receiving the thirty pieces of silver and being turned away from the Sanhedrin, his return in remorse on seeing the crossbeam raised, the councilors’ scorn and the silver thrown on the temple floor, and his death in the valley of Hinnom (186:1.1–1.7); John sent by the Master to bring his mother from Bethany (186:0.1–0.3); John’s arrival as the title was nailed up and his being the only one of the eleven at the cross, his errand into the city for his own mother, the penitent thief, the entrusting of Mary, the sandstorm and the last breath, the centurion’s confession, and the spear in the side (187:2.5–5.8); John remaining at Golgotha (187:6.2); the struggle over the body, the carrying of it to the tomb, and the burial (188:0.3–1.7); the women watching in hiding (188:1.7); the guard at the tomb (188:2.3); and the midnight gathering in the upper room on Saturday (188:3.1–3.2). Taken from earlier papers are the apostles’ hiding places and the debate at the olive press (183:4.2–4.4), the two swords (183:2.2), David’s messengers (186:3.3), the seating and foot washing at the Last Supper (179:1.4–1.5, 179:3), and Thomas’s brief appearance in the upper room (189:4.1).
ch21.b065: Character details come from Paper 139: Judas’s origins and temperament, the breaking point at the anointing, and his fainthearted hope that Jesus would use his power at the last (139:12.10, 12.12); the eleven horrified and stunned at his death, and Jesus regarding him only with pity (139:12.1–12.14); Nathaniel meeting Judas at Tarichea and bringing him (139:12.2), and the words Judas heard at Tarichea (138:5.1); Andrew sensing trouble in Judas and telling no one (139:1.8); Simon Zelotes drawn by the Master’s calm (139:11.5) and his surrender of a high post among the Zealots (138:2.8); Judas’s refusal to confide in his fellows and never going to the Master with a personal problem (193:4.3, 193:4.10). The laying on of hands beginning with Judas and the embrace on the highland are from 140:2.1–2.3.
ch21.b066: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and memories of Judas, John, Simon Zelotes, and Andrew; the scenery of the temple, the valley, and Golgotha; Andrew keeping watch beside his brother at Nicodemus’s house; the apostles taking in Judas’s death in the upper room; and John weeping for Judas. When and through whom news of Judas’s death reached the apostles is not stated in the text and is left open; in light of 191:1.1, where Peter shudders at Judas’s fate on Sunday, it is assumed they knew before then. Judas is drawn not as a villain but as a man who deceived himself.
ch21.b067: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
